explanations.explanation: Cherubim, skillfully worked right into the curtains (Exodus 36:8). That's not a sticker slapped on after the fact. The craftsmen built them into the linen and the blue, purple and scarlet yarn. I once bent a whole batch of cookies trying to make a star look like a star, so I'm impressed.

Lions would make a mighty curtain, I'll give you that. But the text says the curtains have cherubim skillfully worked into them (Exodus 36:8). The linen and the colored yarn are the same, so only the creature changes. Cherubim, friend, not lions.

Palm trees would look nice, but they aren't what the text says goes into these curtains. It says cherubim were skillfully worked into them (Exodus 36:8). The craftsmen are using finely spun linen and blue, purple and scarlet yarn. Remember the cherubim, because they come back later in this passage.

That's the job. The fifty gold clasps join the curtains together, “…so that the tabernacle was a unit.” (Exodus 36:13). Two sets of five curtains go in, and one tabernacle comes out. Fifty little gold clasps, all pulling the same direction, which is more than I can say for my cookie cutters on a busy Saturday.

Good guess, since frames are coming up soon in this passage. But the text says these clasps join the curtains together (Exodus 36:13). Their job is linking the two sets of linen curtains. The result is that the tabernacle is a unit.

Folding sounds practical, and carrying comes up later in this passage. But the text gives the clasps a different job. They join the curtains together, so that the tabernacle was a unit (Exodus 36:13). Fifty gold clasps are linking up those loops.

Six it is. The eleven curtains are joined into one set of five and another of six (Exodus 36:16). Five plus six makes eleven, and I checked it twice on my fingers. My mustache helped with the extra ones.

Five and five is a nice even split, but that only adds up to ten. There are eleven goat hair curtains (Exodus 36:14). So one set has five, and the other set takes the extra curtain and has six (Exodus 36:16).

Seven is close, but the math runs over. Five plus seven would be twelve curtains, and the text says eleven (Exodus 36:14). One set has five, and the other has six (Exodus 36:16). The numbers in this passage are picky, so keep your counting apron on.

Fifty, and the craftsmen kept the pattern. Each set of goat hair curtains gets fifty loops along its edge (Exodus 36:17). That's the same count as the loops on the linen curtains. When something works, you don't change it.
Forty is a respectable number, but it's short by ten. The text says fifty loops along the edge of each set (Exodus 36:17). The linen curtains also had fifty (Exodus 36:12). Fifty again, friend.

Twenty would leave a lot of gaps along that edge. The text says fifty loops on each set of goat hair curtains (Exodus 36:17). That matches the fifty loops on the linen curtains. There's a lot of looping going on in this passage.

True. The veil is made of blue, purple and scarlet yarn and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it (Exodus 36:35). That's the same list of materials as the ten curtains, and the same skillful cherubim. The craftsmen were not about to change a good recipe.

This one is true, so the statement stands. The text says the veil is made of blue, purple and scarlet yarn and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it (Exodus 36:35). Those are the same materials the ten curtains use (Exodus 36:8). So the veil gets the cherubim too.

Silver. The veil's four posts are acacia wood overlaid with gold, and the craftsman cast four silver bases for them (Exodus 36:36). Gold on top and silver on the bottom. The posts are dressed up from head to toe.

Gold is in the picture, but not down at the bottom. The four posts are overlaid with gold, and they have gold hooks (Exodus 36:36). The bases are what the craftsman cast in silver. Gold up top, silver underneath.

Bronze is coming, but not for these posts. The veil's four posts stand on cast silver bases (Exodus 36:36). Bronze bases belong to the five posts at the tent's entrance (Exodus 36:38). The next card has you sorting out exactly that.

Bronze. The entrance has five posts with their hooks, and their five bases were bronze (Exodus 36:38). The veil's posts sit on silver (Exodus 36:36), so the metal changes at the door. Silver inside, bronze at the entrance.

Gold shows up on these posts, just not at the bottom. The tops of the entrance posts and their bands were overlaid with gold (Exodus 36:38). Their five bases were bronze. Keep looking down, friend, because the feet tell the story.

Stone doesn't make an appearance anywhere in the posts here. The text says the five entrance posts stand on bases of bronze (Exodus 36:38). The veil's posts get silver (Exodus 36:36). Every base in this stop is metal.

Carrying. Bezalel, the lead craftsman, makes poles of acacia wood overlaid with gold, and he puts them into the rings on the sides of the ark in order to carry it (Exodus 37:4-5). The gold rings and gold poles are built in from the start. The ark is made to be carried.

Hanging the veil is a different job. The veil hangs on four posts of acacia wood overlaid with gold (Exodus 36:36). The ark's poles slide into rings on its sides in order to carry it (Exodus 37:5). Posts for the veil, poles for the ark.

Holding up frames is a different piece of the story. The frames stand on silver bases (Exodus 36:24). The ark's poles go into the rings on its sides in order to carry it (Exodus 37:5). They're for carrying the ark, friend.
A cherub, one on each end of the mercy seat. Both are hammered gold, and both are made from one piece of gold (Exodus 37:7-8). Hammered, not stuck on. That is a lot of patience with a hammer.

A lion would make a bold seat, but that's not what's there. The text says Bezalel makes two cherubim of hammered gold at the ends of the mercy seat (Exodus 37:7). One is on each end. They're all made from one piece of gold (Exodus 37:8).

An eagle has wings, and so do these, which is probably why it crossed your mind. But the text says two cherubim of hammered gold sit at the ends of the mercy seat (Exodus 37:7). One cherub is on each end, made from one piece of gold (Exodus 37:8).

True. The cherubim had wings that spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat, and they faced each other, looking toward the mercy seat (Exodus 37:9). Wings up, faces toward the middle. Two gold cherubim with their eyes on the same spot.

This one is true, so False doesn't fit. The text says the cherubim had wings that spread upward, overshadowing the mercy seat (Exodus 37:9). It also says they faced each other, looking toward the mercy seat. The craftsmen got every detail right.

That's the list. The utensils for the table are pure gold: plates and dishes, as well as bowls and pitchers for pouring drink offerings (Exodus 37:16). All pure gold, no plain metal in the bunch. My cookie sheets are jealous.

Bells and chains and pomegranates make a fancy list, but they're not what's here. The table's utensils are pure gold plates and dishes, bowls and pitchers for pouring drink offerings (Exodus 37:16). The table gets serving pieces. Plates, dishes, bowls and pitchers is the list to remember.

Censers and snuffers and tongs sound very official, but this isn't that list. The text says the table's utensils are plates and dishes, bowls and pitchers for pouring drink offerings, all pure gold (Exodus 37:16). Everything on the table is for the table. Plates, dishes, bowls and pitchers.

Almond. Each branch gets three cups shaped like almond blossoms, each with buds and petals (Exodus 37:19). That's a lampstand with flowers hammered right into the gold. A lot of detail for something that holds lamps.

Olive is a good guess for a lamp, but the text names a different blossom. The cups are shaped like almond blossoms, each with buds and petals (Exodus 37:19). Three of them go on each branch. Almond is the one.

Fig isn't the blossom here. The text says three cups shaped like almond blossoms go on each branch, each with buds and petals (Exodus 37:19). The same goes for all six branches that extended from the lampstand. Almond, friend.

It doesn't work that way. The text says, “The buds and branches were all of one piece with the lampstand, hammered out of pure gold.” (Exodus 37:22). Nothing was attached afterward. The whole thing came out of one piece of gold.

False is right. The text says, “The buds and branches were all of one piece with the lampstand, hammered out of pure gold.” (Exodus 37:22). No parts were attached afterward. The lampstand is one hammered piece, and I bet that took some arm strength.

Seven. Bezalel also made its seven lamps, its wick trimmers and trays of pure gold (Exodus 37:23). The lamps, trimmers and trays are all pure gold. Seven lamps up there, and I just try to keep one oven light working.

Six is easy to land on, since the lampstand has six branches (Exodus 37:18). But the text says Bezalel made seven lamps (Exodus 37:23). One more than the number of branches. That's a good number to hold onto.
Twelve would make that lampstand a crowded place. The text says seven lamps (Exodus 37:23). They come with wick trimmers and trays of pure gold. Seven, friend, not twelve.

Burning incense. The text calls it the altar of incense (Exodus 37:25), and Bezalel also made the pure, fragrant incense (Exodus 37:29). It's small and square, overlaid with pure gold, with horns that were of one piece with it. A little altar with a lot of gold.

Burnt offerings belong to a different altar. That's the altar of burnt offering, which Bezalel builds in the next chapter, and it's much bigger (Exodus 38:1). This small gold one is the altar of incense (Exodus 37:25). Small and gold for incense, big and bronze for burnt offerings.
Washing hands isn't what the text says for this altar. The text calls it the altar of incense (Exodus 37:25). Bezalel also makes the pure, fragrant incense (Exodus 37:29). So this one is for incense.
A horn at each of the four corners, and the horns and the altar are of one piece (Exodus 38:2). The horns are part of the altar itself, not an add-on. Four corners, four horns.

Cherubim show up a lot in this passage. They're on the curtains, on the veil and on the mercy seat (Exodus 36:8, 36:35, 37:7). But for the altar of burnt offering, the text says Bezalel made a horn at each of the four corners (Exodus 38:2). Horns, not cherubim.

Lamps belong to the lampstand, where Bezalel made seven of them (Exodus 37:23). The altar of burnt offering gets something different at its corners. The text says he made a horn at each of its four corners, so that the horns and altar were of one piece (Exodus 38:2). Horns, not lamps.

Bronze. He overlaid the altar of burnt offering with bronze (Exodus 38:2), and all its utensils are bronze too (Exodus 38:3). The little altar of incense got gold, but this big one gets bronze. Different altar, different metal.
Gold is the covering for the small incense altar (Exodus 37:26). The altar of burnt offering is overlaid with bronze (Exodus 38:2). This one is the big altar. Bronze for the big one, friend.

Silver does plenty of work in this passage, mostly for bases, hooks and bands (Exodus 38:10). But the text says Bezalel overlaid the altar of burnt offering with bronze (Exodus 38:2). Silver doesn't cover this altar. Bronze does.

True. Bezalel cast four rings for the bronze grate and made poles of acacia wood overlaid with bronze. He inserted the poles into the rings on the sides of the altar for carrying it (Exodus 38:5-7). Same plan as the ark and the table. The poles are bronze this time instead of gold.

This one is true, so False doesn't fit. The altar of burnt offering has four cast rings, and poles of acacia wood overlaid with bronze (Exodus 38:5-6). The poles go into the rings on the sides for carrying it (Exodus 38:7). So it matches the ark and the table, with bronze instead of gold.
Not quite. The text says, “He made the altar with boards so that it was hollow.” (Exodus 38:7). So it's built of boards with an empty inside. It isn't solid wood all the way through.

False is right. The text says, “He made the altar with boards so that it was hollow.” (Exodus 38:7). It's built with boards, with room inside. That's one big hollow altar, and I wish my cookie jar were that roomy.

The mirrors. Bezalel made the bronze basin and its stand from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (Exodus 38:8). Nobody would have guessed that one. Shiny mirrors turned into a bronze basin.

Shields would make a lot of bronze, but the text doesn't say that. The bronze for the basin and its stand comes from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (Exodus 38:8). It's a surprising source. Mirrors, friend.

Farm tools make sense for bronze, but they aren't the source here. The text says the basin and its stand were made from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting (Exodus 38:8). The source is the women's mirrors.

Judah. The inventory names Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah (Exodus 38:22). It says he made everything that the LORD had commanded Moses. That's a full name and a tribe, all written down.

Levi is the tribe of the Levites, who recorded the inventory (Exodus 38:21). But the text puts Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, in the tribe of Judah (Exodus 38:22). So the Levites did the writing and Bezalel is from Judah. Two tribes, two jobs.

Benjamin isn't a tribe this passage mentions. The inventory says Bezalel son of Uri, the son of Hur, is of the tribe of Judah (Exodus 38:22). He made everything that the LORD had commanded Moses. Judah is the tribe.

Dan. Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, was with Bezalel as an engraver, designer and embroiderer in blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine linen (Exodus 38:23). That's a long job title for one man. Two tribes working side by side.

Judah is the tribe of Bezalel, not Oholiab (Exodus 38:22). The text says Oholiab son of Ahisamach is of the tribe of Dan (Exodus 38:23). Judah is Bezalel and Dan is Oholiab. Easy to mix up, since they work as a team.

Levi is the tribe of the Levites, who recorded the inventory (Exodus 38:21). Oholiab son of Ahisamach is of the tribe of Dan (Exodus 38:23). He was with Bezalel as an engraver, designer and embroiderer. So the Levites kept the records, and Oholiab came from Dan.
